summary.system: Nuclide Ask (intents, entity resolution, templated cited answers; extractive fallback)
summary.method: For each question: intent from wording rules; records named in the question resolved by longest match over names and aliases; a template per intent fills sentences from those records' structured fields (TL;DR first), each sentence cited; curated benchmark and patient-question pairs supply records when the question matches closely; sentence retrieval (MiniSearch plus concept index, fused) is the fallback and adds detail. The answer text shown on /ask/ is scored for rubric coverage. No language model.

The single most widely used medical radioisotope: a metastable metal with a six-hour lifetime, milked on demand from a bedside generator (a 'moly cow') and attached to a cold kit to image bone, heart, kidneys or lymph nodes. [1] The parent isotope shipped worldwide to make technetium-99m, the gamma-ray tracer used in the majority of nuclear medicine scans. It is made in a handful of ageing research reactors, and when one breaks down, scans get delayed or cancelled. [2] It underpins on the order of tens of millions of scans a year worldwide (bone scans, myocardial perfusion, sentinel lymph node mapping, renal and hepatobiliary studies), each prepared on site by adding the eluted pertechnetate to a lyophilised cold kit. [1] Molybdenum-99 decays with a 65.94-hour (about 2.75-day) half-life to technetium-99m, and its whole purpose in the supply chain is to act as a transportable parent: its longer half-life lets bulk 99Mo be irradiated, processed and shipped internationally to radiopharmacies, which then load it into 99Mo/99mTc generators and elute the six-hour daughter locally, on demand, for the roughly tens of millions of Tc-99m scans performed worldwide each year. [2] A shielded column device lets hospitals 'milk' the world's most-used medical radioisotope, technetium-99m, fresh every day from a longer-lived parent isotope that is shipped to them from a reactor. [3] A version of the PSMA prostate cancer scan that uses the same cheap, widely available radioactive tag as a standard bone scan instead of the PET tracers. [4] It binds prostate-specific membrane antigen on prostate cancer cells; because technetium-99m is a gamma emitter available from any hospital's own generator (unlike gallium-68 or fluorine-18, which need a generator or cyclotron dedicated to PET production), it can be used both for pre-operative SPECT/CT localisation and, with a handheld gamma probe, for intraoperative radioguided surgery. [4]

Like radioligand therapy but with alpha particles: far more destructive over a much shorter range, so single cells can be killed with less collateral damage. [1] There is barely enough of the radioactive metal actinium-225 in the world to treat a few hundred patients a year, even though several new cancer drugs need it. New ways of making it are being built, but they are not yet running at full scale. [2] A metal that fires off very powerful, very short-range radioactive particles as it decays through a chain of daughter atoms. Because the particles barely travel beyond the cell they hit, it can kill a cancer cell while leaving neighbouring healthy cells mostly untouched. Supply is scarce, so it is still mostly used in research studies. [3] Isotope supply (TerraPower, Orano, ITM) is the binding constraint. [1] Actinium-225 dominates targeted alpha therapy pipelines, but lead-212 (from thorium-228/radium-224 generators, used by Orano Med and Perspective Therapeutics), astatine-211 (cyclotron-produced, short half-life, suited to regional supply) and terbium-149 have complementary properties and independent supply routes. [4] Within five years at least two alpha emitters other than actinium-225 reach late-stage trials with GMP supply exceeding clinical demand, and the proportion of alpha therapy trials delayed by isotope supply falls below 10%. [4] Actinium-225 is the alpha-emitting atom behind the most promising next wave of radioligand therapies, and there is not enough of it. [5] RYZ101 is actinium-225 DOTATATE, a targeted alpha therapy: the same SSTR2-binding peptide as Lutathera but chelating 225Ac, whose alpha decay chain delivers dense, short-range double-strand DNA breaks that beta particles cannot match. [6]

The parent isotope shipped worldwide to make technetium-99m, the gamma-ray tracer used in the majority of nuclear medicine scans. It is made in a handful of ageing research reactors, and when one breaks down, scans get delayed or cancelled. [1] The single most widely used medical radioisotope: a metastable metal with a six-hour lifetime, milked on demand from a bedside generator (a 'moly cow') and attached to a cold kit to image bone, heart, kidneys or lymph nodes. [2] Roughly 95% of the world's molybdenum-99 (the parent of technetium-99m, used in about 30 million SPECT scans a year, 80% of all nuclear medicine imaging) comes from a handful of research reactors in South Africa, the Netherlands, Belgium and Australia; because Mo-99's half-life is 66 hours it cannot be stockpiled, so a reactor outage cancels scans within days (OECD-NEA, 2025 review of medical radioisotope supply). [3] Most of the world's therapeutic and scanning isotopes are made by putting targets into about half a dozen ageing research reactors and flying the product out within days. [4] When two reactors were down at once in 2009 and 2010, hospitals worldwide ran short of the most used scan isotope. [4]

Lutetium-177 dotatate was the first modern radioligand therapy (2018), for neuroendocrine tumours, and is now used in first line. [1] A radioactive metal with a one-hour lifetime that is eluted from a shielded generator or made on a cyclotron and attached to a molecule that finds tumours, giving a PET scan the same day. [2] A radioactive metal that gives off short-range radiation. Attached to a molecule that sticks to a tumour, it irradiates the tumour from the inside while sparing most healthy tissue. [3] Gallium-68 decays with a 67.7-minute half-life, mostly by positron emission, and is the diagnostic half of two of the most important theranostic pairs in oncology: 68Ga-DOTATATE/DOTATOC paired with 177Lu-DOTATATE for neuroendocrine tumours, and 68Ga-PSMA-11 paired with 177Lu-PSMA-617 or 225Ac-PSMA for prostate cancer. [2] In people with a slow-growing gut cancer, the radioactive treatment lutetium-177 dotatate did not just shrink tumours for longer - it also kept their day-to-day quality of life, including energy, pain and diarrhoea, better for much longer than the older drug it was compared with. [4] TTD was significantly longer with 177Lu-Dotatate across every domain tested: global health status (HR 0.406), physical functioning (HR 0.518), role functioning (HR 0.580), fatigue (HR 0.621), pain (HR 0.566), diarrhoea (HR 0.473), disease-related worries (HR 0.572) and body image (HR 0.425). [4] China's state-backed isotope and nuclear medicine group: it makes the radioactive material and the medicines that use it. [5] Jonathan Strosberg was principal investigator of NETTER-1, which showed 177Lu-DOTATATE reduces the risk of progression by 79% in midgut neuroendocrine tumours and led to Lutathera's approval, the first radioligand therapy approved for a solid tumour and the template for PSMA-targeted therapy. [6]

A scan that shows where a radioactive tracer accumulates, so it images what tumours are doing rather than what they look like. [1] Positron emission tomography detects the paired 511 keV gamma photons produced when a positron from a radioactive tracer annihilates with an electron; coincidence detection localises the source and the standardised uptake value (SUV) quantifies it. [1] Isotopes such as 18F, 68Ga, 89Zr and 64Cu are attached to a targeting molecule, and the tracer determines what is measured: glucose metabolism (FDG), receptor expression (PSMA, SSTR, TROP2, HER2), stroma (FAP), immune cells (CD8) or DNA repair (PARP). [1] Positron-emitting isotopes (18F, 68Ga, 89Zr, 64Cu) attached to a targeting molecule; coincidence detection of 511 keV photons; standardised uptake value (SUV) quantifies uptake. [1] A short-lived radioactive form of fluorine, made fresh each morning at a local facility, that is attached to a sugar or other small molecule and used for a PET scan. [2] Its 109.8-minute half-life is long enough for a regional cyclotron to make a batch, run it through automated radiochemistry and quality control, and ship unit doses to nearby hospitals, but short enough that the whole chain has to be scheduled tightly around the day's scan list; roughly a third of the activity is lost every hour. [2] Fluorine-18 is made every morning within driving distance of the scanner; gallium-68 comes from either a generator or a cyclotron; copper-64 and zirconium-89 last long enough to ship across a country. [3]

A metal that fires off very powerful, very short-range radioactive particles as it decays through a chain of daughter atoms. Because the particles barely travel beyond the cell they hit, it can kill a cancer cell while leaving neighbouring healthy cells mostly untouched. Supply is scarce, so it is still mostly used in research studies. [1] An extremely short-lived radioactive metal that delivers a powerful, very local burst of radiation. Because it decays away within a few hours, it has to be made freshly at the hospital, right before it is given to the patient. [2] Almost every alpha cancer therapy in development relies on one scarce isotope. [3] Developing several alternatives at once would stop the whole field waiting on a single supply chain. [3] Actinium-225 is the alpha-emitting atom behind the most promising next wave of radioligand therapies, and there is not enough of it. [4] Most of the world's actinium-225, a rare radioactive metal used in some newer cancer treatments, comes from slowly extracting it from an old stockpile of another radioactive element. [5] A different method — firing high-energy protons at ordinary thorium metal in an accelerator — can make much bigger batches, needed if actinium-225 treatments are ever to reach more than a small number of patients. [5]

A radioactive form of the mineral radium that behaves like calcium and settles into bone. It gives off very short-range, high-energy particles that damage cancer growing in bone while barely reaching the healthy marrow next to it. [1] Radium-223 was the first alpha-emitting drug ever approved (2013). [2] It homes to bone like calcium and treats prostate cancer that has spread only to bone. [2] Radium-223, an injected alpha-emitting radioisotope that homes to bone, lengthened survival and delayed skeletal complications in men with castration-resistant prostate cancer that had spread to bone but not to organs. [3] Giving the bone-targeting radiotherapy radium-223 together with the hormone drug abiraterone does not help patients live longer and roughly doubles or triples the risk of a broken bone compared with abiraterone alone. [4] ERA-223 was a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (Smith et al., sponsored by Bayer) in 806 men with asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic bone-predominant metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer, comparing radium-223 plus abiraterone acetate/prednisone/prednisolone against placebo plus abiraterone acetate/prednisone/prednisolone. [4]

A radioactive metal that, once it decays, keeps generating more damaging radioactive particles inside the tumour for weeks. Because it lasts longer than most similar treatments, it can be attached to slow-moving carriers such as full-sized antibodies. [1] Thorium-227 is an alpha emitter with an 18.7-day half-life -- long enough, unlike most alpha emitters, to be conjugated to slow-clearing targeting molecules such as full antibodies rather than only fast peptides. [1] It decays through a five-alpha cascade (via 223Ra, 219Rn, 215Po, 211Pb, 211Bi, 211Po) to stable 207Tl/207Pb, releasing a total of about 32.4 MeV of alpha energy and roughly 0.96 MeV of beta energy per decay chain, making it an in vivo generator of its own daughter, radium-223. [1] A radioactive form of the mineral radium that behaves like calcium and settles into bone. It gives off very short-range, high-energy particles that damage cancer growing in bone while barely reaching the healthy marrow next to it. [2] 227Th is obtained from the same generator/supply chain as radium-223: it is the immediate alpha-decay daughter of actinium-227 (itself made by neutron irradiation of radium-226 in a reactor, 226Ra(n,γ)227Ra → β− → 227Ac), separated from the growing 227Ac/227Th/223Ra generator column. [1]

[2] Radium-223 (https://nuclide.cc/isotopes/ra-223/)

Cancer-seeking molecules carrying the radioactive metal lutetium-177, which delivers short-range radiation to tumours it binds; approved for neuroendocrine tumours and prostate cancer. [1] A radioactive drug that seeks out PSMA on prostate cancer cells; the best-selling radiopharmaceutical ever. [2] A radioactive metal, chemically almost identical to the widely-used lutetium-177, that gives off the same kind of medium-range particles plus a burst of extra very-short-range electrons. Those extra electrons may let it do more damage to a cancer cell than lutetium-177 while using the same delivery molecules. [3] Terbium-161 decays by beta-minus emission with a half-life of 6.95 days (very close to lutetium-177's 6.65 days) to stable dysprosium-161, and shares much of 177Lu's chemistry (both are trivalent lanthanides suited to DOTA-type chelators), so it can be substituted directly into existing DOTATATE, DOTATOC and PSMA-617-type ligands. [3] Terbium-161 is a close chemical cousin of lutetium-177 that, as well as giving off the same kind of radiation, also releases a shower of extremely short-range electrons. [4] In theory that extra radiation could finish off single cancer cells and tiny clusters that a lutetium-177 treatment might miss, using the same targeting molecules already in use. [4] Terbium-161 can replace lutetium-177 in existing PSMA ligands; true nuclear delivery remains preclinical. [5]

The original targeted radiotherapy: thyroid cells soak up iodine, so radioactive iodine destroys leftover thyroid tissue and metastases while sparing everything else. [1] Thyroid cancer is usually curable with surgery and radioactive iodine, the original theranostic. Rare aggressive forms respond to RET and BRAF inhibitors. [2] A radioactive form of iodine. Because the thyroid gland naturally absorbs iodine, swallowing it lets the radiation destroy thyroid cells or thyroid cancer cells almost anywhere they have spread, with very little effect on the rest of the body. [3] A cancer-targeting antibody carrying a radioactive form of iodine was used, as a single course, to treat a type of blood cancer called non-Hodgkin lymphoma. [4] Using the thyroid's natural appetite for iodine to image and treat thyroid cancer with a radioactive form of it. [5]

Tiny plastic beads carrying a radioactive, slightly magnetic metal are injected into the artery feeding a liver tumour. Because the metal shows up on both nuclear scans and MRI, doctors can check exactly where the beads went. [1] Millions of tiny radioactive glass or resin beads are injected into the liver artery, lodging in the tumour and irradiating it from within. [2] Unlike similar beads made with yttrium-90, these can also be seen clearly on a scan. [3] Holmium-166 poly-L-lactic acid (PLLA) microspheres (QuiremSpheres, QuiremScout) deliver radioembolisation to liver tumours much as yttrium-90 microspheres do, but 166Ho's shorter half-life (26.8 hours) concentrates over 90% of the dose within about 4 days, versus roughly 11 days for 90Y. [3]

A radioactive metal that lasts about half a day, long enough to image slower-moving molecules such as antibodies, and chemically identical to copper-67, the isotope used to treat with the same tracer. [1] A radioactive form of copper that pairs with a diagnostic twin made of the same element, copper-64. Using the same metal for the scan and the treatment means the tracer behaves identically both times, which should make dosing more predictable. [2] A copper-based pair uses the identical molecule for both steps, just with a different form of copper, so the scan should be a much truer preview of where the treatment radiation will go. [3] Using the identical molecule for imaging (copper-64) and therapy (copper-67) in PSMA-targeted treatment, rather than switching between different ligands such as gallium-68-PSMA-11 for imaging and lutetium-177-PSMA-617 for therapy, will give a more accurate match between the pre-therapy scan and the actual therapeutic radiation distribution, improving patient selection and predicting toxicity more reliably. [3]

A scan that shows where a radioactive tracer accumulates, so it images what tumours are doing rather than what they look like. [1] FDG PET is the standard PET scan. A radioactive sugar shows which tissues are burning glucose fast, which most cancers do. [2] New whole-body scanners are so much more sensitive than standard PET machines that they can produce a clear picture using a small fraction of the usual radioactive tracer dose. [3] Total-body PET's roughly 40-fold sensitivity gain over conventional PET can be used to cut injected diagnostic tracer activity by 90% or more while preserving diagnostic image quality and lesion detection, reducing radiation dose to patients and staff, rather than being used only to shorten scan duration. [3] FAPI PET is a PET scan that lights up the scaffolding around almost any solid tumour, including cancers the standard sugar scan misses. [4] Neuroblastoma soaks up MIBG, a radioactive cousin of noradrenaline; the Curie and SIOPEN scores count how many body regions still light up on the scan, and a score that has not fallen enough after the first rounds of chemotherapy marks a child who is unlikely to be cured with the standard plan. [5] A panel of cancer and imaging specialists agreed, scenario by scenario, when a PSMA PET scan for prostate cancer is a good idea and when it usually is not - a reference clinicians and insurers use to decide who should get the scan. [6]

Prostate cancer is the home of theranostics: PSMA PET finds it, PSMA radioligands treat it. Hormonal therapy remains the foundation, with PARP and AKT inhibitors added by genotype. [1] A prostate-cancer-specific PET scan that finds spread far earlier than CT or bone scan, and tells you whether a matched radioactive drug will work. [2] How fast PSA is rising matters more than its level: a doubling time under ten months after surgery or radiotherapy, or under nine months in castration-resistant disease, marks the men whose cancer is moving quickly and who benefit from earlier hormone therapy or a PSMA scan, while PSA density (PSA divided by prostate volume) helps decide who needs a biopsy at all. [3] Biochemical recurrence of prostate cancer is a rising PSA after surgery or radiotherapy with nothing yet visible on scans. [4] PSMA PET, with agents such as fluciclovine F-18 and Illuccix, can now find the recurrent disease at very low PSA levels in most men, opening the way to salvage radiation or metastasis-directed therapy. [5] A version of the PSMA prostate cancer scan that uses the same cheap, widely available radioactive tag as a standard bone scan instead of the PET tracers. [6] Fluciclovine F-18 was the first PET tracer approved for finding recurrent prostate cancer after treatment (2016), and has been largely superseded since 2020 by PSMA PET. [7]

A family of usually slow-growing tumours that start in hormone-producing cells of the gut, pancreas and lungs. They pioneered the idea of using the same molecule to see a tumour on a scan and then to treat it with radiation. [1] A PET scan using a radioactive hormone mimic that lights up neuroendocrine tumours and shows whether the matching radioactive treatment will work. [2] FDG PET is the standard PET scan. A radioactive sugar shows which tissues are burning glucose fast, which most cancers do. [3] Grade 3 well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumours divide fast enough to be called grade 3 yet still look and behave like their slower relatives rather than like neuroendocrine carcinoma. [4] Recognised as separate since 2017, they keep the somatostatin receptor, respond less well to platinum chemotherapy, and in the NETTER-2 trial were among the first treated with lutetium-177 dotatate up front. [4] A radioactive drug for neuroendocrine tumours: a small peptide that homes to the somatostatin receptor on the tumour cells carries lutetium-177, which irradiates them from within. [5] Before starting the neuroendocrine tumour treatment Lutathera, patients get a somatostatin-receptor PET scan to confirm the tumour actually has the right target for the drug to lock onto. [6] Radioligand therapy for neuroendocrine tumours built on somatostatin receptor antagonists rather than the agonists used today: antagonists bind the receptor in every state and are not internalised, so they occupy several times more sites per cell and deliver more radiation per dose. [7]

FAPI PET is a PET scan that lights up the scaffolding around almost any solid tumour, including cancers the standard sugar scan misses.
